claims.text: Interface-induced strain and associated microstructural anisotropy govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi nanoscale films or nanoribbons.
Interface-induced strain and microstructural anisotropy broaden the magnetic phase transition.
Controlled thermal annealing reduces residual strain.
Reducing residual strain sharpens the magnetic phase transition.
Reducing residual strain lowers hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The as-deposited material contains significant inherent interfacial strain and microstructural disorder.
An annealing temperature of approximately 300 °C is below the recrystallization temperature of the specified films or nanoribbons.
A mild anneal can partially relieve interfacial strain without inducing large-scale structural changes.
Strain gradients in the as-deposited films alter magnetic-domain configurations.
Strain-gradient-induced changes in magnetic-domain configurations broaden the magnetic phase transition and increase hysteresis.
Thermal annealing produces more uniform grain orientations.
Thermal annealing reduces energy barriers for magnetic switching.
Reduced magnetic-switching barriers narrow the transition and decrease hysteresis.
Post-annealing samples will have a sharper magnetocaloric transition than the as-deposited samples under applied fields below 0.1 T.
Post-annealing samples will have lower hysteresis than the as-deposited samples under applied fields below 0.1 T.
Annealing will yield a more bulk-like magnetocaloric response under low-applied-field conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies when cycle frequency is lower than the rate of structural reconfiguration.
Higher magnetic fields or excessive annealing may cause the results to differ through structural degradation.
